claim: Mutations in KCNC3, which encodes the Kv3.3 K+ channel, cause spinocerebellar ataxia 13 (SCA13).
source: Mutations in KCNC3, which encodes the Kv3.3 K+ channel, cause spinocerebellar ataxia 13 (SCA13).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature establishing this relationship.

claim: SCA13 exists in distinct forms with onset in infancy or adulthood.
source: SCA13 exists in distinct forms with onset in infancy or adulthood.
evidence: This is a well-established clinical observation supported by the literature.

claim: An infant-onset mutation dramatically and transiently increased Purkinje cell excitability.
source: An infant-onset mutation dramatically and transiently increased Purkinje cell excitability, stunted process extension, impaired dendritic branching and synaptogenesis, and caused rapid cell death during cerebellar development.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including electrophysiological recordings and imaging data.

claim: The infant-onset mutation stunted process extension in Purkinje cells.
source: An infant-onset mutation dramatically and transiently increased Purkinje cell excitability, stunted process extension, impaired dendritic branching and synaptogenesis, and caused rapid cell death during cerebellar development.
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis of Purkinje cells expressing the infant-onset mutation.

claim: The infant-onset mutation impaired dendritic branching in Purkinje cells.
source: An infant-onset mutation dramatically and transiently increased Purkinje cell excitability, stunted process extension, impaired dendritic branching and synaptogenesis, and caused rapid cell death during cerebellar development.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of dendritic arbor complexity shown in the figures.

claim: The infant-onset mutation impaired synaptogenesis in Purkinje cells.
source: An infant-onset mutation dramatically and transiently increased Purkinje cell excitability, stunted process extension, impaired dendritic branching and synaptogenesis, and caused rapid cell death during cerebellar development.
evidence: This is supported by observations of reduced dendritic spines and impaired complex spiking.

claim: The infant-onset mutation caused rapid cell death during cerebellar development.
source: An infant-onset mutation dramatically and transiently increased Purkinje cell excitability, stunted process extension, impaired dendritic branching and synaptogenesis, and caused rapid cell death during cerebellar development.
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal imaging data showing disappearance of iR4H-expressing cells.

claim: Reducing excitability increased early Purkinje cell survival in cells expressing the infant-onset mutation.
source: Reducing excitability increased early Purkinje cell survival.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using NS13001 to reduce excitability and subsequent cell counting.

claim: An adult-onset mutation did not significantly alter basal tonic firing in Purkinje cells.
source: In contrast, an adult-onset mutation did not significantly alter basal tonic firing in Purkinje cells, but reduced excitability during evoked high frequency spiking.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings comparing aR3H-expressing cells to controls.

claim: The adult-onset mutation reduced excitability during evoked high frequency spiking.
source: In contrast, an adult-onset mutation did not significantly alter basal tonic firing in Purkinje cells, but reduced excitability during evoked high frequency spiking.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using sudden darkness to evoke high frequency firing.

claim: Purkinje cells expressing the adult-onset mutation matured normally.
source: Purkinje cells expressing the adult-onset mutation matured normally and did not degenerate during cerebellar development.
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis showing normal dendritic arbor development.

claim: Purkinje cells expressing the adult-onset mutation did not degenerate during cerebellar development.
source: Purkinje cells expressing the adult-onset mutation matured normally and did not degenerate during cerebellar development.
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal imaging showing persistent survival of aR3H-expressing cells.

claim: Differential changes in the excitability of cerebellar neurons contribute to the distinct ages of onset in infant- and adult-onset SCA13.
source: Our results suggest that differential changes in the excitability of cerebellar neurons contribute to the distinct ages of onset and timing of cerebellar degeneration in infant- and adult-onset SCA13.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Differential changes in the excitability of cerebellar neurons contribute to the timing of cerebellar degeneration in infant- and adult-onset SCA13.
source: Our results suggest that differential changes in the excitability of cerebellar neurons contribute to the distinct ages of onset and timing of cerebellar degeneration in infant- and adult-onset SCA13.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Spinocerebellar ataxias (SCAs) are a group of rare, autosomal dominant diseases characterized by locomotor deficits and cerebellar degeneration.
source: Spinocerebellar ataxias (SCAs) are a group of rare, autosomal dominant diseases characterized by locomotor deficits and cerebellar degeneration, typically with onset in adulthood (Klockgether et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: SCAs typically have onset in adulthood.
source: Spinocerebellar ataxias (SCAs) are a group of rare, autosomal dominant diseases characterized by locomotor deficits and cerebellar degeneration, typically with onset in adulthood (Klockgether et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Spinocerebellar ataxia 13 (SCA13) is caused by mutations in the KCNC3 gene.
source: Spinocerebellar ataxia 13 (SCA13) is caused by mutations in the KCNC3 gene, which encodes the Kv3.3 voltage-gated K+ channel (Waters et al., 2006; Figueroa et al., 2010; Figueroa et al., 2011; Duarri et al., 2015; Zhang and Kaczmarek, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The KCNC3 gene encodes the Kv3.3 voltage-gated K+ channel.
source: Spinocerebellar ataxia 13 (SCA13) is caused by mutations in the KCNC3 gene, which encodes the Kv3.3 voltage-gated K+ channel (Waters et al., 2006; Figueroa et al., 2010; Figueroa et al., 2011; Duarri et al., 2015; Zhang and Kaczmarek, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: SCA13 exists in two forms that differ in the age of onset and associated symptoms.
source: Unlike most SCAs, SCA13 exists in two forms that differ in the age of onset and associated symptoms (Herman-Bert et al., 2000; Waters et al., 2005; Waters et al., 2006; Figueroa et al., 2010; Figueroa et al., 2011; Duarri et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to clinical literature.

claim: The early-onset form of SCA13 is evident in infancy with motor delay, persistent motor deficits, and intellectual disability.
source: The early-onset form is evident in infancy with motor delay, persistent motor deficits, and intellectual disability (Herman-Bert et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to clinical literature.

claim: Severe cerebellar maldevelopment and atrophy have been observed by MR imaging by 10 months of age in early-onset SCA13.
source: Severe cerebellar maldevelopment and atrophy have been observed by MR imaging by 10 months of age (Khare et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to clinical imaging studies.

claim: The adult-onset form of SCA13 typically emerges in the third or fourth decade of life with progressive ataxia.
source: In contrast, the adult-onset form typically emerges in the third or fourth decade of life with progressive ataxia accompanied by progressive degeneration of the cerebellum (Subramony et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to clinical literature.

claim: The adult-onset form of SCA13 is accompanied by progressive degeneration of the cerebellum.
source: In contrast, the adult-onset form typically emerges in the third or fourth decade of life with progressive ataxia accompanied by progressive degeneration of the cerebellum (Subramony et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to clinical literature.

claim: The infant- and adult-onset forms of SCA13 are caused by distinct mutations in Kv3.3.
source: The infant- and adult-onset forms of SCA13 are caused by distinct mutations in Kv3.3 (Waters et al., 2006; Figueroa et al., 2010; Figueroa et al., 2011; Duarri et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genetic studies.

claim: The age of onset in SCA13 is strongly correlated with the same mutation in unrelated families.
source: The age of onset is strongly correlated with the same mutation in unrelated families, indicating that the two forms of SCA13 do not reflect differences in genetic background (Waters et al., 2006; Figueroa et al., 2010; Figueroa et al., 2011; Duarri et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genetic studies.

claim: The two forms of SCA13 do not reflect differences in genetic background.
source: The age of onset is strongly correlated with the same mutation in unrelated families, indicating that the two forms of SCA13 do not reflect differences in genetic background (Waters et al., 2006; Figueroa et al., 2010; Figueroa et al., 2011; Duarri et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that the same mutation causes the same phenotype in unrelated families.

claim: Infant- and adult-onset mutations have differential effects on Kv3.3 function.
source: We have shown that infant- and adult-onset mutations have differential effects on Kv3.3 function that may underlie the two forms of the disease (Waters et al., 2006; Minassian et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: The adult-onset mutation R420H does not generate functional channels when expressed alone.
source: An adult-onset mutation, R420H, which changes the third arginine in the S4 transmembrane segment to histidine, does not generate functional channels when expressed alone (Waters et al., 2006; Minassian et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous functional studies.

claim: R420H changes the third arginine in the S4 transmembrane segment to histidine.
source: An adult-onset mutation, R420H, which changes the third arginine in the S4 transmembrane segment to histidine, does not generate functional channels when expressed alone (Waters et al., 2006; Minassian et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a description of the mutation location and nature.

claim: Upon co-assembly with wild-type subunits, the R420H mutant subunit suppresses Kv3.3 activity by a dominant negative mechanism.
source: Upon co-assembly with wild-type subunits in the tetrameric channel, the mutant subunit suppresses Kv3.3 activity by a dominant negative mechanism (Minassian et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous functional studies.

claim: Under physiological conditions, the functional properties of the residual current from R420H do not differ significantly from wild type.
source: Under physiological conditions, the functional properties of the residual current do not differ significantly from wild type (Minassian et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous functional studies.

claim: Several infant-onset mutations, including R423H, have dominant gain-of-function effects on channel gating.
source: In contrast, several infant-onset mutations, including R423H, which changes the fourth arginine in S4 to histidine, have dominant gain-of-function effects on channel gating, with or without an accompanying dominant negative effect (Waters et al., 2006; Minassian et al., 2012; Duarri et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous functional studies.

claim: R423H changes the fourth arginine in S4 to histidine.
source: In contrast, several infant-onset mutations, including R423H, which changes the fourth arginine in S4 to histidine, have dominant gain-of-function effects on channel gating, with or without an accompanying dominant negative effect (Waters et al., 2006; Minassian et al., 2012; Duarri et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the mutation location and nature.

claim: Infant-onset mutations may have an accompanying dominant negative effect in addition to gain-of-function effects.
source: In contrast, several infant-onset mutations, including R423H, which changes the fourth arginine in S4 to histidine, have dominant gain-of-function effects on channel gating, with or without an accompanying dominant negative effect (Waters et al., 2006; Minassian et al., 2012; Duarri et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous functional studies.

claim: Kv3.3 has specialized gating properties that shape the functional repertoire of neurons.
source: This is significant because Kv3.3, like other Kv3 family members, has specialized gating properties that shape the functional repertoire of neurons (Rudy and McBain, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Kv3 channels supported by citation.

claim: Kv3.3 activates in a depolarized voltage range normally attained only during action potentials.
source: Kv3.3 activates in a depolarized voltage range normally attained only during action potentials (Rudy and McBain, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Kv3.3 gating supported by citation.

claim: Kv3.3 does not contribute significantly to maintaining the resting potential or modulating excitability near threshold.
source: As a result, the channel does not contribute significantly to maintaining the resting potential or modulating excitability near threshold.
evidence: This is an inference from the voltage dependence of Kv3.3 activation.

claim: During an action potential, Kv3.3 channels open with fast kinetics, leading to rapid repolarization.
source: During an action potential, Kv3.3 channels open with fast kinetics, leading to rapid repolarization, brief spikes, and efficient recovery of voltage-gated Na+ channels from inactivation (Rudy and McBain, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Kv3.3 function supported by citation.

claim: Kv3.3 activation leads to brief spikes during action potentials.
source: During an action potential, Kv3.3 channels open with fast kinetics, leading to rapid repolarization, brief spikes, and efficient recovery of voltage-gated Na+ channels from inactivation (Rudy and McBain, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Kv3.3 function supported by citation.

claim: Kv3.3 activation leads to efficient recovery of voltage-gated Na+ channels from inactivation.
source: During an action potential, Kv3.3 channels open with fast kinetics, leading to rapid repolarization, brief spikes, and efficient recovery of voltage-gated Na+ channels from inactivation (Rudy and McBain, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Kv3.3 function supported by citation.

claim: Upon repolarization, Kv3.3 channels close quickly, shortening the afterhyperpolarization.
source: Upon repolarization, Kv3.3 channels close quickly, shortening the afterhyperpolarization and facilitating the next action potential (Rudy and McBain, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Kv3.3 function supported by citation.

claim: Quick closure of Kv3.3 channels facilitates the next action potential.
source: Upon repolarization, Kv3.3 channels close quickly, shortening the afterhyperpolarization and facilitating the next action potential (Rudy and McBain, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Kv3.3 function supported by citation.

claim: The gating properties of Kv3.3 promote sustained, high frequency firing of action potentials in neurons.
source: These gating properties promote sustained, high frequency firing of action potentials in neurons (Rudy and McBain, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Kv3.3 function supported by citation.

claim: Kv3.3 is highly expressed in cerebellar Purkinje cells.
source: Kv3.3 is highly expressed in cerebellar Purkinje cells, where it contributes to the mechanism of spontaneous pacemaking (Martina et al., 2003; Akemann and Knöpfel, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Kv3.3 contributes to the mechanism of spontaneous pacemaking in Purkinje cells.
source: Kv3.3 is highly expressed in cerebellar Purkinje cells, where it contributes to the mechanism of spontaneous pacemaking (Martina et al., 2003; Akemann and Knöpfel, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Kv3.3 is co-expressed in Purkinje cells with the Nav1.6 voltage-gated Na+ channel.
source: Kv3.3 is co-expressed in Purkinje cells with the Nav1.6 voltage-gated Na+ channel (Raman et al., 1997; Khaliq et al., 2003; Martina et al., 2003; Akemann and Knöpfel, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: During an action potential, Nav1.6 is subject to open channel block conferred by an auxiliary subunit.
source: During an action potential, Nav1.6 is subject to open channel block conferred by an auxiliary subunit thought to be Navβ4 or FGF14 (Grieco et al., 2005; White et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The auxiliary subunit conferring open channel block on Nav1.6 is thought to be Navβ4 or FGF14.
source: During an action potential, Nav1.6 is subject to open channel block conferred by an auxiliary subunit thought to be Navβ4 or FGF14 (Grieco et al., 2005; White et al., 2019).
evidence: This is current understanding based on cited literature.

claim: Rapid repolarization mediated by Kv3.3 relieves open channel block of Na+ channels, generating a resurgent Na+ current.
source: Rapid repolarization mediated by Kv3.3 relieves open channel block of Na+ channels, generating a resurgent Na+ current in the interspike interval that triggers the next action potential (Raman and Bean, 1997; Khaliq et al., 2003; Grieco et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of pacemaking supported by citations.

claim: The resurgent Na+ current occurs in the interspike interval and triggers the next action potential.
source: Rapid repolarization mediated by Kv3.3 relieves open channel block of Na+ channels, generating a resurgent Na+ current in the interspike interval that triggers the next action potential (Raman and Bean, 1997; Khaliq et al., 2003; Grieco et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of pacemaking supported by citations.

claim: Kv3.3 and Nav1.6 together regulate the spontaneous tonic firing that is characteristic of Purkinje cells.
source: Together, these channels regulate the spontaneous tonic firing that is characteristic of Purkinje cells (Raman et al., 1997; Khaliq et al., 2003; Martina et al., 2003; Akemann and Knöpfel, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The locomotor deficits in SCA13 are primarily cerebellar in origin.
source: The locomotor deficits in SCA13 are primarily cerebellar in origin (Stevanin et al., 2005; Waters and Pulst, 2008; Subramony et al., 2013; Klockgether et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The aR3H mutation corresponds to R420H in human Kv3.3 and R335H in zebrafish Kv3.3.
source: The aR3H mutation corresponds to R420H and R335H in human and zebrafish Kv3.3, respectively (Mock et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The iR4H mutation corresponds to R423H in human Kv3.3 and R338H in zebrafish Kv3.3.
source: The iR4H mutation corresponds to R423H and R338H in human and zebrafish Kv3.3, respectively (Mock et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Zebrafish Purkinje cells are born on the 3rd day post-fertilization.
source: We have previously shown that zebrafish Purkinje cells, which are born on the 3rd day post-fertilization (Bae et al., 2009), become spontaneously active within hours, coinciding with the expression of Kv3.3 and Nav1.6, ion channels that regulate spontaneous pacemaking activity in mammalian Purkinje cells (Hsieh et al., 2014; Raman and Bean, 1997; Khaliq et al., 2003; Martina et al., 2003; Akemann and Knöpfel, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Zebrafish Purkinje cells become spontaneously active within hours of birth.
source: We have previously shown that zebrafish Purkinje cells, which are born on the 3rd day post-fertilization (Bae et al., 2009), become spontaneously active within hours, coinciding with the expression of Kv3.3 and Nav1.6, ion channels that regulate spontaneous pacemaking activity in mammalian Purkinje cells (Hsieh et al., 2014; Raman and Bean, 1997; Khaliq et al., 2003; Martina et al., 2003; Akemann and Knöpfel, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The onset of spontaneous activity in zebrafish Purkinje cells coincides with the expression of Kv3.3 and Nav1.6.
source: We have previously shown that zebrafish Purkinje cells, which are born on the 3rd day post-fertilization (Bae et al., 2009), become spontaneously active within hours, coinciding with the expression of Kv3.3 and Nav1.6, ion channels that regulate spontaneous pacemaking activity in mammalian Purkinje cells (Hsieh et al., 2014; Raman and Bean, 1997; Khaliq et al., 2003; Martina et al., 2003; Akemann and Knöpfel, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The frequency and regularity of tonic firing in zebrafish Purkinje cells increase until ~5 days post-fertilization.
source: The frequency and regularity of tonic firing increase until ~5 days post-fertilization (dpf) and then remain stable through at least 14 dpf (Hsieh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Tonic firing in zebrafish Purkinje cells remains stable through at least 14 dpf.
source: The frequency and regularity of tonic firing increase until ~5 days post-fertilization (dpf) and then remain stable through at least 14 dpf (Hsieh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: By 5 dpf, most zebrafish Purkinje cells exhibit complex spiking in response to synaptic input from climbing fibers.
source: By 5 dpf, most cells also exhibit complex spiking in response to synaptic input from climbing fibers originating in the inferior olive (Hsieh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Climbing fibers originate in the inferior olive.
source: By 5 dpf, most cells also exhibit complex spiking in response to synaptic input from climbing fibers originating in the inferior olive (Hsieh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established neuroanatomical knowledge.

claim: The properties of tonic action potential firing and complex spiking in Purkinje cells are similar in zebrafish and mammals.
source: The properties of tonic action potential firing and complex spiking in Purkinje cells are similar in zebrafish and mammals (Hsieh et al., 2014; Sengupta and Thirumalai, 2015; Scalise et al., 2016; Harmon et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to comparative studies.

claim: The iR4H and aR3H subunits are non-functional in the absence of wild-type Kv3 channel subunits.
source: It is important to note that the iR4H and aR3H subunits are non-functional in the absence of wild-type Kv3 channel subunits.
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies and data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The aR3H mutation introduced into mammalian or zebrafish Kv3.3 is non-functional when expressed alone.
source: This has been demonstrated for the aR3H mutation introduced into either mammalian or zebrafish Kv3.3 by expression and voltage clamp analysis in Xenopus oocytes (Waters et al., 2006; Minassian et al., 2012; Mock et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: The iR4H mutation introduced into mammalian Kv3.3 is non-functional when expressed alone.
source: It has also been shown for the iR4H mutation introduced into mammalian Kv3.3 (Figueroa et al., 2010; Minassian et al., 2012), a finding that we have now confirmed for iR4H in zebrafish Kv3.3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations and data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The iR4H mutation in zebrafish Kv3.3 is non-functional when expressed alone.
source: It has also been shown for the iR4H mutation introduced into mammalian Kv3.3 (Figueroa et al., 2010; Minassian et al., 2012), a finding that we have now confirmed for iR4H in zebrafish Kv3.3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutant aR3H and iR4H subunits must co-assemble with endogenous wild-type Kv3 subunits to affect Purkinje cell excitability.
source: Accordingly, these mutant subunits would have to co-assemble with endogenous, wild-type Kv3 subunits to affect Purkinje cell excitability.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the observation that mutant subunits are non-functional alone.

claim: Expression of the iR4H mutation dramatically increased Purkinje cell excitability soon after the emergence of spontaneous tonic firing at ~3.5 dpf.
source: Expression of the iR4H mutation dramatically increased Purkinje cell excitability soon after the emergence of spontaneous tonic firing at ~3.5 dpf (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: By 3.75 dpf, a few iR4H-expressing neurons were firing at an unusually high frequency.
source: By 3.75 dpf, a few iR4H-expressing neurons were firing at an unusually high frequency (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The fraction of iR4H-expressing cells that were hyperexcitable increased dramatically by 4 dpf.
source: The fraction of iR4H-expressing cells that were hyperexcitable increased dramatically by 4 dpf (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: By 4.25 dpf, there was relatively little overlap in the range of average firing frequencies seen in control and iR4H-expressing cells.
source: By 4.25 dpf, there was relatively little overlap in the range of average firing frequencies seen in control and iR4H-expressing cells (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and supplementary figures.

claim: By 4.25 dpf, most iR4H-expressing cells fired intermittently, with high frequency bouts of action potential spiking separated by intervals of reduced activity.
source: Although a substantial fraction of iR4H-expressing cells exhibited sustained tonic firing at 4 dpf, by 4.25 dpf, most fired intermittently, with high frequency bouts of action potential spiking separated by intervals of reduced activity (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by representative traces shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The hyperexcitability of iR4H-expressing Purkinje cells was transient.
source: The hyperexcitability of iR4H-expressing Purkinje cells was transient.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that most cells fell silent by 5.25 dpf.

claim: By 5.25 dpf, most iR4H-expressing cells had fallen silent.
source: By 5.25 dpf, most cells expressing iR4H had fallen silent (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Between 5 and 7 dpf, fewer than 5–10% of iR4H-expressing cells fired action potentials.
source: In contrast, between 5 and 7 dpf, fewer than 5–10% of iR4H-expressing cells fired action potentials.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the electrophysiological recordings.

claim: iR4H-expressing cells that continued to fire between 5 and 7 dpf did so at abnormally high frequencies.
source: Those that continued to fire did so at abnormally high frequencies (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: In control Purkinje cells, functional climbing fiber input from inferior olive neurons was first observed at 3.75 dpf.
source: In control Purkinje cells, functional climbing fiber input from inferior olive neurons was first observed at 3.75 dpf when a minority of cells (~17%) fired complex spikes.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the electrophysiological recordings.

claim: At 3.75 dpf, approximately 17% of control Purkinje cells fired complex spikes.
source: In control Purkinje cells, functional climbing fiber input from inferior olive neurons was first observed at 3.75 dpf when a minority of cells (~17%) fired complex spikes.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Complex spiking in control Purkinje cells increased to ~37% by 4.25 dpf.
source: This increased to ~37% by 4.25 dpf and ~70% by 5.25 dpf (Figure 1B; Hsieh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Complex spiking in control Purkinje cells increased to ~70% by 5.25 dpf.
source: This increased to ~37% by 4.25 dpf and ~70% by 5.25 dpf (Figure 1B; Hsieh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the electrophysiological recordings.

claim: No complex spikes were recorded from iR4H-expressing cells at 3.75 dpf.
source: In contrast, no complex spikes were recorded from a comparable number of iR4H-expressing cells at 3.75 dpf, and only ~17% fired complex spikes at 4.25 dpf.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Only ~17% of iR4H-expressing cells fired complex spikes at 4.25 dpf.
source: In contrast, no complex spikes were recorded from a comparable number of iR4H-expressing cells at 3.75 dpf, and only ~17% fired complex spikes at 4.25 dpf.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the electrophysiological recordings.

claim: No complex spiking was observed in iR4H-expressing cells at 5.25 dpf.
source: No complex spiking was observed at 5.25 dpf, in accord with the observation that most iR4H-expressing Purkinje cells were electrically silent by that time.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Expression of the adult-onset aR3H mutation did not significantly alter the excitability of Purkinje cells under basal conditions.
source: In contrast to iR4H, expression of the adult-onset aR3H mutation did not significantly alter the excitability of Purkinje cells under basal conditions (Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The average frequency of spontaneous tonic firing did not differ significantly in aR3H-expressing and control cells between 4.25 and 8.25 dpf.
source: The average frequency of spontaneous tonic firing did not differ significantly in aR3H-expressing and control cells between 4.25 and 8.25 dpf (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Complex spiking emerged normally in aR3H-expressing neurons.
source: Complex spiking emerged normally in aR3H-expressing neurons, with no significant difference in frequency compared to control cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Expression of exogenous wild-type Kv3.3 did not alter the frequencies of tonic firing in Purkinje cells compared to controls.
source: Similarly, expression of exogenous wild-type Kv3.3 did not alter the frequencies of tonic firing or complex spiking in Purkinje cells compared to controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Expression of exogenous wild-type Kv3.3 did not alter the frequencies of complex spiking in Purkinje cells compared to controls.
source: Similarly, expression of exogenous wild-type Kv3.3 did not alter the frequencies of tonic firing or complex spiking in Purkinje cells compared to controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Reducing Kv3 activity with channel blockers or by genetic deletion of Kcnc genes in mice impairs sustained fast spiking.
source: Previous work indicates that reducing Kv3 activity with channel blockers or by genetic deletion of Kcnc genes in mice impairs sustained fast spiking due to the increased accumulation of Na+ channel inactivation (Erisir et al., 1999; Lau et al., 2000; Akemann and Knöpfel, 2006; Rudy and McBain, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Impaired sustained fast spiking due to reduced Kv3 activity is caused by increased accumulation of Na+ channel inactivation.

claim: Expression of the dominant negative aR3H subunit significantly decreases the excitability of Kv3.3-expressing CaP motor neurons in the zebrafish spinal cord.

claim: In response to depolarizing current injection, aR3H-expressing motor neurons fail to maintain spiking throughout the pulse.
source: In response to depolarizing current injection, aR3H-expressing motor neurons fail to maintain spiking throughout the pulse, unlike control cells.

claim: The effect of aR3H on motor neuron excitability is more prominent at higher firing frequencies.

claim: Decreased excitability in aR3H-expressing motor neurons is correlated with a reduction in the amplitude of outward currents.

claim: The zebrafish cerebellum receives visual input via mossy fiber pathways by 4 dpf.

claim: Mossy fibers activate parallel fibers, which in turn synapse on Purkinje cells.
source: Mossy fibers activate parallel fibers, which in turn synapse on Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is established neuroanatomical knowledge.

claim: By 4 dpf, sudden darkness leads to a dramatic increase in tonic firing frequency in the majority of medially-located Purkinje cells.
source: We have shown that by 4 dpf, sudden darkness leads to a dramatic increase in tonic firing frequency in the majority of medially-located Purkinje cells (Hsieh et al., 2014).

claim: In control cells, the firing rate remains elevated for several seconds after the sudden darkness stimulus and then gradually returns to the original tonic firing frequency.

claim: In some aR3H-expressing cells, the recovery phase led to prolonged cessation of firing.
source: However, during the recovery phase of the response, the firing rate in aR3H-expressing cells fell below the original firing frequency, in some cases leading to prolonged cessation of firing (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: aR3H-expressing Purkinje cells have a latent hypoexcitability that is revealed after an interval of evoked, high frequency firing.
source: We conclude that aR3H-expressing Purkinje cells have a latent hypoexcitability that is revealed after an interval of evoked, high frequency firing.

claim: In humans, cerebellar development extends into the first postnatal year.
source: In humans, cerebellar development extends into the first postnatal year.

source: In infant-onset SCA13, cerebellar maldevelopment and degeneration are evident by 10 months of age (Khare et al., 2017).

claim: By 3.25 dpf, Purkinje cells had begun to extend processes.

source: Dendrites could be identified unambiguously by the presence of a high density of spines starting at 3.75 dpf.

claim: Postsynaptic development in Purkinje cells is well correlated with functional innervation.
source: These results indicate that postsynaptic development is well correlated with functional innervation of Purkinje cells, which receive active parallel fiber inputs from cerebellar granule cells by 4 dpf (Hsieh et al., 2014).

claim: Purkinje cells receive active parallel fiber inputs from cerebellar granule cells by 4 dpf.
source: These results indicate that postsynaptic development is well correlated with functional innervation of Purkinje cells, which receive active parallel fiber inputs from cerebellar granule cells by 4 dpf (Hsieh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Functional climbing fiber input from inferior olive neurons begins to emerge at 4 dpf.

evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

source: The complex morphology of Purkinje cells was maintained on subsequent days with ongoing growth and refinement of the dendritic arbor (Figure 4A; Video 1).

claim: Purkinje cells expressing the infant-onset iR4H mutation began to extend processes on schedule on the 3rd day post-fertilization.

evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4B and Video 2.

claim: The density of spines was dramatically decreased in iR4H-expressing Purkinje cells compared to control cells.
source: The density of spines was dramatically decreased compared to control cells, indicating that iR4H severely disrupted postsynaptic development.

claim: iR4H severely disrupted postsynaptic development in Purkinje cells.
source: The density of spines was dramatically decreased compared to control cells, indicating that iR4H severely disrupted postsynaptic development.

claim: The relative lack of dendritic spines may contribute to impaired complex spiking in iR4H-expressing Purkinje cells.

source: In contrast, the development of aR3H-expressing Purkinje cells was similar to control cells.

source: By 4 dpf, Purkinje cells expressing the adult-onset mutation had elaborated complex dendritic arbors studded with spines (Figure 4C; Video 3).

claim: Dendritic morphology was maintained on subsequent days in aR3H-expressing Purkinje cells.
source: Dendritic morphology was maintained on subsequent days.

source: When first observed at 3.25 dpf, total process length and the complexity of the dendritic arbor, measured as the number of branches, did not differ significantly between Purkinje cells expressing mEGFP, aR3H, iR4H, or exogenous wild-type Kv3.3 (Figure 5A,B).

claim: When first observed at 3.25 dpf, the complexity of the dendritic arbor did not differ significantly between Purkinje cells expressing mEGFP, aR3H, iR4H, or exogenous wild-type Kv3.3.
source: When first observed at 3.25 dpf, total process length and the complexity of the dendritic arbor, measured as the number of branches, did not differ significantly between Purkinje cells expressing mEGFP, aR3H, iR4H, or exogenous wild-type Kv3.3 (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: At 3.25 dpf, iR4H-expressing cells already had the shortest processes and the least complex dendritic arbors.
source: However, iR4H-expressing cells already had the shortest processes and the least complex dendritic arbors.
evidence: This is an observation from the quantitative analysis.

source: Starting at 3.75 dpf, total process length and the number of branches were reduced significantly in iR4H-expressing cells compared to cells in the other groups.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis and statistical testing.

claim: Starting at 3.75 dpf, the number of branches was reduced significantly in iR4H-expressing cells compared to cells in the other groups.
source: Starting at 3.75 dpf, total process length and the number of branches were reduced significantly in iR4H-expressing cells compared to cells in the other groups.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis and statistical testing.

claim: Process length and branch number in Purkinje cells expressing aR3H, exogenous wild-type Kv3.3, or mEGFP did not differ significantly from each other.
source: In contrast, process length and branch number in Purkinje cells expressing aR3H, exogenous wild-type Kv3.3, or mEGFP did not differ significantly from each other, although there was a trend for aR3H-expressing cells to have shorter processes and fewer branches by 6.25 dpf.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis and statistical testing.

claim: There was a trend for aR3H-expressing cells to have shorter processes and fewer branches by 6.25 dpf.
source: In contrast, process length and branch number in Purkinje cells expressing aR3H, exogenous wild-type Kv3.3, or mEGFP did not differ significantly from each other, although there was a trend for aR3H-expressing cells to have shorter processes and fewer branches by 6.25 dpf.
evidence: This is an observation from the quantitative analysis.

claim: Maldevelopment of Purkinje cells was specific to the infant-onset mutation.
source: These data indicate that maldevelopment of Purkinje cells was specific to the infant-onset mutation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the comparative data.

claim: The number of spines did not differ significantly in Purkinje cells expressing mEGFP, aR3H, or exogenous wild-type Kv3.3 between 5.25 and 7.25 dpf.
source: The number of spines did not differ significantly in Purkinje cells expressing mEGFP, aR3H, or exogenous wild-type Kv3.3 between 5.25 and 7.25 dpf (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: There was substantial variation in the numbers of spines in individual Purkinje cells.
source: There was, however, substantial variation in the numbers of spines in individual cells, which may reflect the dynamic formation and pruning of synapses that occur during cerebellar development.
evidence: This is an observation from the quantitative analysis.

claim: The variation in spine numbers may reflect the dynamic formation and pruning of synapses during cerebellar development.
source: There was, however, substantial variation in the numbers of spines in individual cells, which may reflect the dynamic formation and pruning of synapses that occur during cerebellar development.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed variation.

claim: The range of spine numbers in cells expressing mEGFP, aR3H, or exogenous wild-type Kv3.3 overlapped.
source: However, the range of values in cells expressing mEGFP, aR3H, or exogenous wild-type Kv3.3 overlapped (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: There is no evidence that expression of the adult-onset mutation impaired postsynaptic development.
source: Therefore, we did not find evidence that expression of the adult-onset mutation or exogenous wild-type Kv3.3 impaired postsynaptic development, in contrast to the infant-onset iR4H mutation (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the spine counting data.

claim: There is no evidence that expression of exogenous wild-type Kv3.3 impaired postsynaptic development.
source: Therefore, we did not find evidence that expression of the adult-onset mutation or exogenous wild-type Kv3.3 impaired postsynaptic development, in contrast to the infant-onset iR4H mutation (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the spine counting data.

claim: The scarcity of dendritic spines on iR4H-expressing cells indicates that the infant-onset mutation markedly disrupts postsynaptic development.
source: The scarcity of dendritic spines on iR4H-expressing cells indicates that the infant-onset mutation markedly disrupts postsynaptic development (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the imaging data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: iR4H dramatically reduced branching of the dendritic arbor.
source: In parallel, iR4H dramatically reduced branching of the dendritic arbor (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The formation of stable branches in neuronal processes is mechanistically linked to synapse formation in both the pre- and postsynaptic compartments in zebrafish.
source: Previous work in zebrafish indicates that the formation of stable branches in neuronal processes is mechanistically linked to synapse formation in both the pre- and postsynaptic compartments (Niell et al., 2004; Meyer and Smith, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In developing optic tectum neurons in zebrafish, postsynaptic specializations form on newly extended dendritic filopodia.
source: In developing optic tectum neurons in zebrafish, postsynaptic specializations form on newly extended dendritic filopodia.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: If a synapse is maintained on a dendritic filopodium, the filopodium develops into a stable dendritic branch.
source: If the synapse is maintained, the filopodium develops into a stable dendritic branch (Niell et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Presynaptic development and branching of the terminal axonal arbor are tightly correlated in retinal ganglion cells in zebrafish.
source: Similarly, presynaptic development and branching of the terminal axonal arbor are tightly correlated in retinal ganglion cells in zebrafish (Meyer and Smith, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Synapses develop on nascent branches in retinal ganglion cells.
source: Synapses develop on nascent branches.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: If a stable synapse is not formed on a nascent branch, the branch is retracted.
source: If a stable synapse is not formed, the branch is retracted.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: CaP cells are fast-spiking neurons that endogenously express Kv3.3.
source: Like Purkinje cells, CaP cells are fast-spiking neurons that endogenously express Kv3.3 (Issa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Kv3.3 is expressed in motor neurons in mammals.
source: Similarly, Kv3.3 is expressed in motor neurons in mammals (Brooke et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Expression of the infant-onset iR4H mutation dramatically reduced the number of synapses in the axonal compartment of CaP neurons compared to neurons expressing aR3H or EGFP alone.
source: Expression of the infant-onset iR4H mutation dramatically reduced the number of synapses in the axonal compartment compared to CaP neurons expressing the adult-onset aR3H mutation or EGFP alone (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The number of synapses in CaP neurons expressing aR3H did not differ significantly from EGFP controls.
source: In contrast, the number of synapses in CaP neurons expressing aR3H did not differ significantly from EGFP controls.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis and statistical testing.

claim: The axons of iR4H-expressing motor neurons had significantly fewer distal branches than the other groups.
source: Furthermore, the axons of iR4H-expressing motor neurons had significantly fewer distal branches than the other groups (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,D; Figure 5—figure supplement 2), reminiscent of reduced dendritic branching in iR4H-expressing Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Reduced axonal branching in iR4H-expressing CaP neurons is reminiscent of reduced dendritic branching in iR4H-expressing Purkinje cells.
source: Furthermore, the axons of iR4H-expressing motor neurons had significantly fewer distal branches than the other groups (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,D; Figure 5—figure supplement 2), reminiscent of reduced dendritic branching in iR4H-expressing Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is a comparative observation.

claim: The length of the distal branches in iR4H-expressing CaP neurons did not differ significantly from those in EGFP-expressing motor neurons.
source: The length of the distal branches that were present in iR4H-expressing CaP neurons did not differ significantly from those in EGFP-expressing motor neurons, although they were significantly shorter than those in aR3H-expressing cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The distal branches in iR4H-expressing CaP neurons were significantly shorter than those in aR3H-expressing cells.
source: The length of the distal branches that were present in iR4H-expressing CaP neurons did not differ significantly from those in EGFP-expressing motor neurons, although they were significantly shorter than those in aR3H-expressing cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The length of distal branches in aR3H-expressing neurons and EGFP controls did not differ significantly.
source: In contrast, the length of distal branches in aR3H-expressing neurons and EGFP controls did not differ significantly.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis and statistical testing.

claim: The paucity of distal branches in iR4H-expressing CaP neurons was not due to a failure of axonal outgrowth.
source: The paucity of distal branches in iR4H-expressing CaP neurons was not due to a failure of axonal outgrowth because the length of the main axon shaft did not differ significantly in motor neurons expressing iR4H, aR3H, or EGFP alone (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,F; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that main axon length was normal.

claim: The length of the main axon shaft did not differ significantly in motor neurons expressing iR4H, aR3H, or EGFP alone.
source: The paucity of distal branches in iR4H-expressing CaP neurons was not due to a failure of axonal outgrowth because the length of the main axon shaft did not differ significantly in motor neurons expressing iR4H, aR3H, or EGFP alone (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,F; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Reductions in presynaptic specializations and distal branching in iR4H-expressing CaP neurons both reflect significantly impaired synaptogenesis.
source: Given the relationship between synaptogenesis and branching in zebrafish neurons (Niell et al., 2004; Meyer and Smith, 2006), our results suggest that reductions in presynaptic specializations and distal branching in iR4H-expressing CaP neurons are not independent phenomena. Rather, both effects likely reflect significantly impaired synaptogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about the relationship between synaptogenesis and branching.

claim: The iR4H mutation disrupts both pre- and post-synaptic development.
source: Taken together, our results in Purkinje cells and CaP motor neurons indicate that the iR4H mutation disrupts both pre- and post-synaptic development, impairing the formation of stable branches in the axonal and dendritic arbors, respectively.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined data from Purkinje cells and motor neurons.

claim: The iR4H mutation impairs the formation of stable branches in the axonal and dendritic arbors.
source: Taken together, our results in Purkinje cells and CaP motor neurons indicate that the iR4H mutation disrupts both pre- and post-synaptic development, impairing the formation of stable branches in the axonal and dendritic arbors, respectively.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined data from Purkinje cells and motor neurons.

claim: The number of proximal axonal branches was similar in CaP neurons expressing EGFP, iR4H, or aR3H.
source: Although the number of these branches was similar in all three groups, the proximal branches in iR4H-expressing cells were significantly longer than those seen in CaP neurons expressing aR3H or EGFP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G,H; Figure 5—figure supplement 2 ).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The proximal branches in iR4H-expressing CaP cells were significantly longer than those in cells expressing aR3H or EGFP.
source: Although the number of these branches was similar in all three groups, the proximal branches in iR4H-expressing cells were significantly longer than those seen in CaP neurons expressing aR3H or EGFP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G,H; Figure 5—figure supplement 2 ).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The effects of the iR4H mutation on proximal and distal branching in CaP axons were similar to those of another infant-onset mutation, F448L (iFL).
source: Interestingly, the effects of the iR4H mutation on proximal and distal branching in CaP axons were similar to those of another infant-onset mutation, F448L (iFL) (Figure 1A; Issa et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a comparative observation supported by citation to previous work.

claim: iFL-expressing CaP neurons have fewer distal branches than control cells.
source: iFL-expressing CaP neurons also have fewer distal branches than control cells and extend long, aberrant proximal collaterals (Issa et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: iFL-expressing CaP neurons extend long, aberrant proximal collaterals.
source: iFL-expressing CaP neurons also have fewer distal branches than control cells and extend long, aberrant proximal collaterals (Issa et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The iFL mutation causes dominant changes in Kv3.3 gating similar to those of iR4H.
source: The iFL mutation causes dominant changes in Kv3.3 gating similar to those of iR4H, but iFL does not have an accompanying dominant negative effect (Minassian et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous functional studies.

claim: iFL does not have an accompanying dominant negative effect.
source: The iFL mutation causes dominant changes in Kv3.3 gating similar to those of iR4H, but iFL does not have an accompanying dominant negative effect (Minassian et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous functional studies.

claim: Altered gating and resulting changes in excitability underlie the similar effects of iR4H and iFL on CaP development.
source: Therefore, it is likely that altered gating and resulting changes in excitability underlie the similar effects of these two infant-onset mutations on CaP development.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of the two mutations.

claim: iR4H-expressing Purkinje cells disappeared during cerebellar development in vivo.

source: This striking phenotype was highly penetrant.

source: By 5 dpf, one third of the iR4H-expressing Purkinje cells that had been imaged at 4 dpf were no longer visible, and by 6 dpf, more than 80% of the cells had vanished.

claim: By 6 dpf, more than 80% of iR4H-expressing Purkinje cells had vanished.
source: By 5 dpf, one third of the iR4H-expressing Purkinje cells that had been imaged at 4 dpf were no longer visible, and by 6 dpf, more than 80% of the cells had vanished.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the longitudinal imaging data.

claim: Two iR4H-expressing Purkinje cells persisted until 7 dpf.

claim: One iR4H-expressing Purkinje cell was still visible at 8 dpf prior to disappearing.
source: Two cells persisted until 7 dpf, one of which was still visible at 8 dpf prior to disappearing.
evidence: This is an observation from the longitudinal imaging data.

claim: Acridine orange staining signifies the activation of cell death pathways.

evidence: This is established knowledge about acridine orange staining supported by citation.

claim: Purkinje cells expressing aR3H, exogenous wild-type Kv3.3, or mEGFP showed no evidence of net process retraction or atrophy through 8 dpf.
source: In contrast to iR4H-expressing cells, all Purkinje cells expressing aR3H, exogenous wild-type Kv3.3, or mEGFP alone that were imaged at 3.75 dpf remained visible through 8 dpf, the latest time point examined, with no evidence of net process retraction or atrophy (Figure 6A, see Figure 4A,C, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: Expression of the infant-onset mutation, but not the adult-onset mutation or exogenous wild-type Kv3.3, resulted in rapid Purkinje cell death during cerebellar development in vivo.

source: The age-dependent degeneration of iR4H-expressing Purkinje cells in zebrafish is reminiscent of the early postnatal degeneration of the cerebellum that occurs in infant-onset SCA13 patients (Khare et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparative observation linking the zebrafish model to human disease.
